title: Reciprocal facilitation between ants and small mammals
citation: Canepuccia AD, Hidalgo FJ, Fanjul E, Iribarne OO. Reciprocal facilitation between ants and small mammals in tidal marshes. Oecologia. 2024 Mar;204(3):575-588.
methods_summary: Canepuccia conducted a series of factorial experiments to investigate how ant mounds from fire ants (Solenopsis richteri) and cavy (Cavia apera) droppings independently and interactively alter sediment quality and facilitate plant growth in marsh ecosystems. They selected 20 active ant mounds and 20 control plots (without mounds) in the middle of the marsh. Over a period of three weeks, half of the plots (both with and without mounds) received 10 cavy droppings weekly, while the remaining plots served as “no-dropping” control mounds. After three weeks, sediment samples were collected from a depth of 7 cm. In ant mound plots, samples were taken from both the center and the edge of the mound. In the laboratory, these samples were analyzed for water content (% H2O), organic matter (% OM), and three key nutrients: ammonium (NH4+), nitrate (NO3–), and phosphate (PO43–). The data was then analyzed using Two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD tests to identify significant differences in soil chemistry across the treatment combinations, and is shown in Figure 3. Figure 4 presents the growth ratios of cordgrass (Spartina densiflora) plants that were transported in subsequent experiments. The presence of ant mounds and cavy droppings were manipulated as in the previous experiment (Figure 3).
interpretation_notes: Figure 3 illustrates characteristics of the sediment based on ant mound lcation and cavy dropping presence. The figure compares from three locations: the center of the ant mound, the edge of the ant mound, and the sediment far from the mounds. The lowercase letters (a, b, and a,b) represent statistical groupings that indicate significant differences among the ant mound treatments (Center ant-mound, Next ant-mound, and Sediment). If two bars or boxes have different letters (e.g., one is "a" and another is "b"), it means there is a statistically significant difference between those treatments. If two treatments share the same letter (e.g., both are "a"), there is no significant difference between them. A treatment labeled with "a,b" is statistically similar to both the treatments labeled "a" and those labeled "b." Greek letters (?,?) are used to indicate statistical differences between the cavy droppings treatments (Droppings vs. No droppings). The labels "Cavies" and "Cavies exclusion" in Figure 4 represent the experimental manipulation of large herbivore access, however there was no significant effect of cavy presence (herbivory) on the initial growth ratios themselves.

title: Salamanders regulate top-down effects
citation: Hickerson, C. M., Anthony, C. D., & Walton, B. M. (2017). Eastern red-backed salamanders regulate top-down effects in a temperate forest-floor community. Herpetologica, 73(3), 180-189.
methods_summary: Over the course of 4 years, Hickerson and researchers conducted a predator removal experiment in a mixed deciduous forest in Ohio. This study utilized an unfenced feild design consisting of 32 plots, each containing 9 artifical cover objects (AOCs). Focal predars were removed by hand during weekly to biweekly visits. Figure 2 specifically compares plots with the most salamanders (CR) and those with the fewest salamanders (SR) and how they regulate the abundance of macrodetritivores on the forest floor. The researchers used ANOVA to compare the mean numbers of invertebrates across treatments. To meet the assumptions of the statistical tests, data were log10(x+1) transformed, and Dunnett T3 post hoc tests were applied to account for unequal variance among groups.
interpretation_notes: The figure labels the treatments as CR and SR, which represent a gradient of salamander density rather than the complete removal of a single species. CR represents Centipede Removal which resulted in the greatest density if salamanders. SR represents Salamander Removal which maintained the lowest density of salamanders. The "mean number of" counts on the y-axis represent the mean number of taxa observed per replicate over a 4 year period on the x-axis.

title: Spatial heterogeneity of soil biochar content
citation: Olmo M, Lozano AM, Barrón V, Villar R. Spatial heterogeneity of soil biochar content affects soil quality and wheat growth and yield. Sci Total Environ. 2016 Aug 15;562:690-700.
methods_summary: In 2013, researchers applied biochar to experimental field plots at the “Origuero” farm near Córdoba, southern Spain, with the goal of creating an initially uniform biochar distribution across the soil surface. During the first growing season, sunflowers were grown for four months as the first crop in a rotation. At the end of the season, the field was plowed. This disturbance, combined with earlier sunflower sowing, redistributed the biochar unevenly. Wheat was then planted in the plots using a row-seed drill. At 142 days after sowing, wheat was harvested and plant performance was quantified using response variables such as aboveground biomass and grain production. To test whether wheat growth differed across the biochar distribution categories, the researchers used a one-way ANOVA comparing outcomes among BC-content levels.
interpretation_notes: Before wheat germination, researchers observed strong variation in biochar coverage and therefore classified each plot into a visual biochar distribution (Visual-BC) category ranging from 0 to 4. Category 0 represented a control plot with no biochar, while categories 1–4 represented increasing biochar surface coverage (1 = <20% coverage, 4 = >60% coverage). The letters (A, B, C, D) above the bars indicate the results of the Tukey post-hoc test; bars sharing a letter are not statistically different, while different letters indicate significant shifts between categories. Above each chart, the Spearman correlation coefficient (rs) and its significance level (one asterisk indicates a significance level of P<0.05, two asterisks indicates a significance level of P<0.01, and three asterisks indicates a significance level of P<0.001, representing the highest level of statistical significance in the study) quantify the overall strength of the relationship across all five categories.

title: Photosynthetic light response curve of cacao
citation: de Santana EN, Kuhlcamp KT, Crasque J, Cerri Neto B, Oliveira VS, Dousseau-Arantes S. Photosynthetic Light Response Curve and Photosynthetic Performance of Cacao (Theobroma cacao L.) Genotypes Grown Under Full Sun Field Conditions. Plants (Basel). 2025 Nov 21;14(23):3555.
methods_summary: Cocoa (Theobroma cacao L.), an understory tree, has traditionally been cultivated in shaded systems. However, full sun cultivation has been expanding due to its higher yield potential, earlier harvests, and improved fruit quality. Moreover, some genotypes of Cocoa have shown better adaptation to high light intensities than others. The response to full sun varies among genotypes, necessitating the selection of more light-tolerant machinery that can withstand high irradiance. Initially, exposure to high irradiance may enhance the photosynthetic rate and productive potential of cacao trees. However, several studies indicate that intense light and elevated temperatures can lead to photoinhibition, reducing the physiological performance of plants. In 2025, researchers in Brazil examined the net photosynthetic rate (Pn) of eleven cacao genotypes grown in full sun. Net photosynthetic response curves as a function of photosynthetically active photon flux density were fitted for the eleven cacao genotypes using a hyperbolic model, providing insights into the varying responses of these genotypes to light intensity.
interpretation_notes: The paper provides the evolutionary context that Theobroma cacao is naturally an understory tree. This information is vital because it explains why "full sun" is considered a stressor in the first place; the study is essentially testing how well a shade-loving species can be "forced" into a high-productivity, high-radiation environment.

title: Optimal patch residence time in egg parasitoids
citation: Boivin G, Fauvergue X, Wajnberg E. Optimal patch residence time in egg parasitoids: innate versus learned estimate of patch quality. Oecologia. 2004 Mar;138(4):640-7.
methods_summary: The fairyfly wasp (Anaphes victus) is an egg parasitoid of weevils, including the carrot weevil (Listronotus oregonensis), a significant pest of plants in the carrot family. In 2004, scientists at the Plant Research and Innovation Center (CRIV) in Quebec, Canada, observed the patch-leaving behavior of female fairyfly wasps under varying environmental conditions. In the experiment, females were presented with a patch of 16 carrot weevil eggs, and two primary variables were manipulated: patch quality and travel time. Patch quality was controlled by adjusting the initial proportion of hosts already parasitized by another female (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%), while travel time was approximated by isolating the females for either a short delay (3 hours) or a long delay (48 hours) between emergence and patch encounter. Each treatment was replicated 15 times, and the researchers used video recordings to measure the total patch residence time, which was defined as the duration from the moment the female entered the patch until she abandoned it for more than 60 seconds. These results were then plotted to illustrate how the wasps adjusted their stay based on the costs and benefits predicted by the Marginal Value Theorem.
interpretation_notes: The figure requires the interpreter to understand that superparasitism (ovipositing in an already parasitized host) results in a lower fitness gain, which is why the parasitized hosts represent lower patch "quality". While this is explained in the paper, it is a specific biological detail not covered in the general animal behavior lecture, or by the figure alone.

title: Character displacement in flying stag beetles
citation: Zhang SN, Kubota K. Strongly exclusive distribution with putative character displacement in two flying stag beetles. Evolution. 2023 Jan 23;77(1):155-165
methods_summary: In 2002, researchers in Japan compared the body length (BL) of male and female P. takakuwai and P. viridicuprus stag beetles, collected from two distinct geographic contexts. The first was a narrow contact area consisting of 28 sites, and the second were broader allopatric regions represented by 26 sites. For each beetle, body length was defined as the linear distance from the anterior margin of the labrum (upper lip) to the end of the elytra (hardened forewing). Because these beetles exhibit sexual dimorphism, the morphological data for males (A) and females (B) were analyzed independently. The researchers employed an Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) followed by post-hoc Tukey’s tests to evaluate significant differences in body size between populations and generate figure 4.
interpretation_notes: Interpreting the x-axis requires understanding that the "Allopatric region" refers to areas where each species lives in isolation, while the "Contact area" refers to the narrow parapatric zone where the two species meet and potentially interact. It is also necessary to recognize that stag beetles are sexually dimorphic, meaning males and females naturally have different body sizes; therefore, the data for males (A) and females (B) must be interpreted independently. Finally, the lowercase letters (a, b, c) above the boxes indicate statistically significant differences based on post-hoc Tukey’s tests; populations sharing the same letter are not significantly different from one another, regardless of their species.

title: Divergent gametic thermal performance and floral warming across an elevation gradient.
citation: Heiling JM, Koski MH. Divergent gametic thermal performance and floral warming across an elevation gradient. Evolution. 2024 Mar 26;78(4):665-678.
methods_summary: Researchers evaluated the reproductive thermal ecology of the Silverweed forb, Argentina anserina, collected from six populations across a 1000 m elevation gradient in Colorado. Cloned plants from three high-elevation and three low-elevation sites were exposed to seven growth chamber temperature treatments spanning 0–39 °C. Performance was quantified using three metrics: pollen germination proportion, mean pollen tube length, and seed set. The researchers used the minpack.lm package in R to construct Gaussian thermal performance curves (TPCs) for each trait, which allowed them to estimate the thermal optimum (Topt) and the 50% tolerance breadth (B50). These parameters are represented in Figure 3 by the peak of each curve and the width of the dashed horizontal lines, respectively.
interpretation_notes: Students must identify that the top row of charts represents high-elevation populations, while the bottom row represents low-elevation populations. Also, the figure caption explicitly notes that Y-axis ranges differ among populations to highlight the shape of the curves. Students must be cautioned to look at the numbers on the Y-axis carefully; for instance, a peak in one population might represent a much lower absolute performance level than a peak in another, even if they look similar.

title: Climate and aridity measures relationships with spectral vegetation indices across desert fringe shrublands in the South-Eastern Mediterranean Basin
citation: Shoshany, Maxim, and Sofia Mozhaeva. “Climate and aridity measures relationships with spectral vegetation indices across desert fringe shrublands in the South-Eastern Mediterranean Basin.” Environmental monitoring and assessment vol. 195,5 563. 13 Apr. 2023.
methods_summary: Researchers analyzed climatic fluctuations across a Mediterranean to arid transition zone in the Mediterranean Basin between 2015 and 2018. Monthly rainfall and temperature data were obtained from the Israel Meteorological Service for three primary meteorological stations: Beit Jamal, Lahav, and Beer Sheva. Using these inputs, the researchers calculated Potential Evapotranspiration (PET), accounting for average monthly temperature, day length, and a calculated heat index. The Water Deficit (WD) was then calculated by taking the difference between monthly rainfall and PET. The resulting values were plotted over three years to illustrate the region's water balance.
interpretation_notes: Compared to typical Walter-Leith Climate Diagrams, this figure is more abstract. Figure 2 plots a single calculated variable, the Water Deficient, which is the difference between rainfall and potential evapotranspiration (PET), on one axis. Instead of searching for line intersections, students must look for crossings of the zero line. Positive values indicate a surplus, while negative values indicate a deficit.

title: Dispersal, patch leaving, and distribution of Homalodisca vitripennis (Hemiptera: Cicadellidae)
citation: Northfield, T. D., Mizell, R. F., 3rd, Paini, D. R., Andersen, P. C., Brodbeck, B. V., Riddle, T. C., & Hunter, W. B. (2009). Dispersal, patch leaving, and distribution of Homalodisca vitripennis (Hemiptera: Cicadellidae). Environmental entomology, 38(1), 183–191. https://doi.org/10.1603/022.038.0123
methods_summary: The glassy-winged sharpshooter (Homalodisca vitripennis) is the primary vector of the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa, which is responsible for Pierce’s Disease in grapes. Since its invasion of California in the late 1980s, this insect has resulted in significant economic losses for California vineyards. Researchers in Northern Florida conducted studies to analyze dispersal patterns and patch-leaving behavior of this vector to enhance the prediction of bacterium spread within cropping systems and to develop effective control measures. To generate the data for Figure 3, researchers conducted mark-release-recapture experiments using H. vitripennis adults in patches of high-quality (Lagerstroemia indica) and low-quality (Prunus persica) host plants. The insects were marked with aerosol hair dye and released at the center of each plot, and were then monitored using sticky traps checked at increasing intervals of time. To calculate the “population half-life” for each release date, the researchers applied an exponential decay model to the number of insects recaptured per hour.
interpretation_notes: Students must be told extra information regarding the nutrition of each host used in the experiment; crape myrtle (Lagerstroemia indica) is a nutritionally superior host, while peach (Prunus persica) is a lower-quality host. Also, the term "population half-life" is used as a quantitative proxy for patch residence time. Students should be told that this value represents the specific point in time when 50% of the released individuals have left the patch. By calculating this single number for each release date, researchers can statistically compare "stay times" across different years and host species.

title: Seedling size affects the strategy of dune seedlings responding to rainfall variation
citation: Shen-Tu, X. L., Hu, Y. K., Shea, K., Gascoigne, S. J. L., Wei, Q., Tang, L. C., Li, D. D., & Li, S. L. (2025). Seedling size affects the strategy of dune seedlings responding to rainfall variation. Annals of botany, 135(6), 1125–1134. https://doi.org/10.1093/aob/mcaf017
methods_summary: Researchers collected large (likely autumn-germinated) and small (likely spring-germinated) seedlings of the dominant desert shrub Artemisia ordosica from a field site in the Mu Us Desert, China. The seedlings were transplanted into individual pots and kept under a transparent plastic roof to ensure that all water intake was strictly controlled through experimental irrigation. The seedlings were tested on a gradient of seven rainfall intensities ranging from -75% to +75% of the 15-year monthly average to simulate varying levels of drought and water surplus. After 96 days, the researchers harvested the plants and separated them into leaves, stems, and roots, determined their dry mass, and calculated the root–shoot ratio. They then used statistical models to test how starting seedling size influenced how plants adjusted their biomass allocation under different moisture conditions.
interpretation_notes: Students must understand the root–shoot ratio to the resource allocation trade-offs, specifically the balance between acquiring water using roots and light using shoots. Also students must recognize that negative x-axis values signify drought stress, resulting in mortality at the -75% treatment. The data also illustrates a fundamental difference in phenotypic plasticity: large seedlings significantly shift their strategy toward drought tolerance as water decreases, while small seedlings maintain a fixed strategy prioritizing competitive growth for light (which is why no line for small seedlings is shown for panel G).

title: Predicting prey population dynamics from kill rate, predation rate and predator-prey ratios in three wolf-ungulate systems
citation: Vucetich, J.A., Hebblewhite, M., Smith, D.W. and Peterson, R.O. (2011), Predicting prey population dynamics from kill rate, predation rate and predator–prey ratios in three wolf-ungulate systems. Journal of Animal Ecology, 80: 1236-1245. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2656.2011.01855.x
methods_summary: To generate the data for Panel D in Figure 4, researchers analyzed 41 years (1971–2011) of empirical observations from the Isle Royale moose–wolf system. Isle Royale is an isolated single predator–single prey system where wolves are the sole predator of moose. The dependent variable, annual prey growth rate (rt), was calculated for each year using the formula rt =(Nt+1−Nt)/Nt, where moose abundance (N) was estimated annually through aerial surveys using fixed-wing aircraft and cohort analysis. The independent variable, predation rate (PR), represents the proportion of the moose population killed by wolves. A linear regression was fitted to the resulting annual data points.
interpretation_notes: Difficulties may arise when interpreting that annual prey growth rate is equivalent to the intrinsic growth rate seen in Population Growth equations represented by r. Annual prey growth rate is simply the "real-world version" of the intrinsic growth rate used in the Lotka-Volterra equations. The researchers use annual prey growth rate ​to measure the actual growth rate achieved by moose or elk in the face of real wolves.

title: Biological properties and vector competence of Diaphorina citri for Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus modulated by an insect-specific virus
citation: Galdeano, D. M., Rawat, T., Ingram, W., Carlson, C. R., Alves, G. R., & Kuo, Y. W. (2025). Biological properties and vector competence of Diaphorina citri for Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus modulated by an insect-specific virus. iScience, 28(8), 112982. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2025.112982
methods_summary: Asian citrus psyllids vector the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas), the causal agent for the plant pathogen Citrus Greening Disease. Researchers at the Contained Research Facility at UC Davis, California compared two California populations of Diaphorina citri, the Asian citrus psyllid. One population was persistently infected with the insect-specific virus DcFLV and one DcFLV-uninfected (virus-free) control group. Their experimental setup involved placing pairs of adult psyllids consisting of one male and one female onto Citrus macrophylla cuttings with young flush shoots. These cuttings were held in water-filled 50 mL tubes and confined within mesh cages in a climate-controlled greenhouse maintained at 27±2 °C with a 14:10 (Light:Dark) hour photoperiod. The researchers observed the insects daily until death to record the survival and total lifespan of each individual. Survival rates were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method to generate the curves shown in panels A, C, E, and G, while longevity was quantitatively compared using two-tailed unpaired t-tests in panels B, D, F, and H to identify statistically significant differences
interpretation_notes: The insect specific virus (DcFLV) in the experiment influences the insect host behavior, such as delaying development and increasing feeding behavior without significantly reducing the fitness of the psyllid vector. This neutral effect on host fitness is likely driven by the virus's reliance on vertical transmission, and killing the host would end the virus's own transmission line.

title: Coextistence of two amphibian species is predicted by analysis of isoclines
citation: Gazzola, A., Van Buskirk, J. Isocline analysis of competition predicts stable coexistence of two amphibians. Oecologia 178, 153–159 (2015). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-015-3273-y
methods_summary: Researchers tested the interaction between two anuran (frog & toad) amphibian species, in mesocosms (an experimental system meant to replicate natural conditions, under researcher control) meant to replicate as close as possible conditions seen in nature. Mesocosms included leaf litter, rabbit food, and were seen to support the life of a variety of microorganisms. Tadpoles were then added from five separate rounds of reproduction of each species.
interpretation_notes: This figure shows the density numbers of two species of amphibians as tadpoles, both individually and alone. The authors did not clarify what the number above each dot on the graph was.

title: The coexistence of shortgrass species is mediated by inter- and intraspecific competition
citation: Aguiar, M. R., Lauenroth, W. K., & Peters, D. P. (2001). Intensity of Intra- and Interspecific Competition in Coexisting Shortgrass Species. Journal of Ecology, 89(1), 40–47. http://www.jstor.org/stable/3072116
methods_summary: Researchers used a homogenous and heterogenous quadrats of coexisting shortgrasses to test whether the theory that stable existence between similar species is possible when intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific. The study was conducted in two separate experiments, with a small homogenous community over three years and a larger heterogenous community over two.
interpretation_notes: BG and BD are each species of shortgrass, standing for Bouteloua gracilis and Buchloe dactyloides, respectively. +C represents conditions with more competition, and -C conditions with less.

title: Trophic cascade caused by fishing leads to collapse of a salt-marsh ecosystem
citation: Altieri, A. H., Bertness, M. D., Coverdale, T. C., Herrmann, N. C., & Angelini, C. (2012). A trophic cascade triggers collapse of a salt-marsh ecosystem with intensive recreational fishing. Ecology, 93(6), 1402–1410.
methods_summary: Researchers surveyed northwestern Atlantic salt marshes at 14 different sites. They used observation (counting anglers), historical records, and experiment, where they used trapping and netting to catch predators and herbivores and examining their numbers. The goal was to find out if increased fishing pressure in the salt marshes was causing a trophic cascade/collapse.
interpretation_notes: This data was taken from interactions between populations in salt marshes. Examine each figure to interpret the full picture.

title: Indirect increased predation on native organisms by invasive prey
citation: Castorani, M. C. N., & Hovel, K. A. (2015). Invasive prey indirectly increase predation on their native competitors. Ecology, 96(7), 1911–1922. http://www.jstor.org/stable/43494942
methods_summary: Researchers manipulated density in plotted areas of both native bivalves and a prolific invasive bivalve, Arcuatula. Density treatments were applied randomly to different plots. This was to test how interactions between invasive species and predators affect native densities and recruitment. As well as decreasing each other's densities through competition, it was found that the invasive bivalves indirectly negatively affect native species by increasing predator attraction.
interpretation_notes: Arcuatula senhousia effects on two native bivalve species, Chione undatella and Laevicardium substratum.

title: Climate change is affecting the outcomes of multi-mutualist interactions
citation: Magnoli, S. M., Keller, K. R., & Lau, J. A. (2023). Mutualisms in a warming world: How increased temperatures affect the outcomes of multi-mutualist interactions. Ecology, 104(3), 1–12. https://www.jstor.org/stable/27256077
methods_summary: Using both ambient and elevated temperatures, researchers tested how changes in temperature affected plant biomass, with involvements between multi-mutualisms between rhizobium, plants, defensive ants, and pollinators.
interpretation_notes: The experiment itself was testing the effects of increased temperatures on these interactions, but this specific figure doesn't include this.

title: Resilience in stochastic systems
citation: Ives, A. R. (1995). Measuring Resilience in Stochastic Systems. Ecological Monographs, 65(2), 217–233. https://doi.org/10.2307/2937138
methods_summary: Researchers were looking to measure resilience (time taken to return to equilibrium after disturbances) in a stochastic system. They used simulated population density data sets, over various time series.
interpretation_notes: No extra interpretation necessary.

title: Climate change is affecting the outcomes of multi-mutualist interactions
citation: Magnoli, S. M., Keller, K. R., & Lau, J. A. (2023). Mutualisms in a warming world: How increased temperatures affect the outcomes of multi-mutualist interactions. Ecology, 104(3), 1–12. https://www.jstor.org/stable/27256077
methods_summary: Using both ambient and elevated temperatures, researchers tested how changes in temperature affected plant biomass, with involvements between multi-mutualisms between rhizobium, plants, defensive ants, and pollinators.
interpretation_notes: The left graph shows plant biomass under various conditions and the right shows produced seed number.

title: How predators decrease prey population growth through changes in prey behavior
citation: Nelson, E.H., Matthews, C.E. and Rosenheim, J.A. (2004), PREDATORS REDUCE PREY POPULATION GROWTH BY INDUCING CHANGES IN PREY BEHAVIOR. Ecology, 85: 1853-1858. https://doi.org/10.1890/03-3109
methods_summary: Researchers wanted to investigate how predators can reduce prey populations through inducing changes in behavior. They used both normal and surgically-altered predators (who could not eat the prey but could still interact with them), as well as aphids as prey. The results showed that the hugest disturbance/ reduction in numbers was by normal predators who consumed and disturbed the aphids, as well as a large decrease in aphid numbers by predators who could disturb only. They reduce dnumbers by causing a change in the behavior of the aphids, who spent less time feeding in the presence of damsel bugs, and so tended to survive less.
interpretation_notes: Damsel bug effect on aphid reproduction (left graphs) and behavior (right graphs) at different conditions (not-present [none] disturbance-only [surgically modified damsel bugs], and normal). Results in experiment 1 on the left side were non-significant, the results in experiment 2 were significant.

title: The implications for landscape management due to forest fragmentation
journal: Landscape Ecology in Forest Management and Conservation
citation: Bogaert, J. et al. (2011). Forest Fragmentation: Causes, Ecological Impacts and Implications for Landscape Management. In: Li, C., Lafortezza, R., Chen, J. (eds) Landscape Ecology in Forest Management and Conservation. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-12754-0_12
methods_summary: Two separate experiments, one using an analysis of forest diversity in the Tanda region's Ivory Coast, as well as studying edge effects on rodents in Kisangani in the Democratic Republic of the Congo- to fully understand the effects of fragmentation.
interpretation_notes: Number of patches per grid is effectively the level of fragmentation in that area.

title: Interspecific interactions are interrupted by light and noise pollution
citation: McMahon, T. A., Rohr, J. R., & Bernal, X. E. (2017). Light and noise pollution interact to disrupt interspecific interactions. Ecology, 98(5), 1290–1299. http://www.jstor.org/stable/26165217
taxa: Insects; Diptera; Midges; Amphibians; Anura; Frogs
methods_summary: Researchers were curious how noise and light pollution affect certain interspecific interactions, such as between the frog-biting midge, and the host it parasitizes, the tungara frog. Researchers surveyed sites where tungara frogs have been observed calling, and found that while noise/light pollution has little effect on the frogs, it does significantly negatively impact the midges.
interpretation_notes: Each dot shape correlates to a different level of city noise, and the x-axis varying levels of light. The left figure shows the effects of these variable on number of midges present. The right figures show the results of how easily the midges could locate a frog's call that the researchers placed inside of a container, again at different city noise and light levels.

title: Fragmentation effects on reproduction in four woodland plant species
citation: Cunningham, S.A. (2000), Effects of Habitat Fragmentation on the Reproductive Ecology of Four Plant Species in Mallee Woodland. Conservation Biology, 14: 758-768. https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1523-1739.2000.98609.x
methods_summary: Researchers were interested in the effects of fragmentation on the make-up of the community, particularly in relation to pollinators, resource availability, mates, and etc. The scientist examined the reproduction of a few species of trees in New South Wales, Australia, with resulting variation in fragmentation affect among species. Fragmentation mainly affected these species through changes in reproduction and changes in interactions with animals.
interpretation_notes: Notice that the x-axis is on logarithmic scale.

title: Non-Random Foraging by Hummingbirds
citation: Wolf, L. L., & Hainsworth, F. R. (1990). Non-Random Foraging by Hummingbirds: Patterns of Movement Between Ipomopsis aggregata (Pursch) V. Grant Inflorescences. Functional Ecology, 4(2), 149–157.
methods_summary: Researchers wanted to examine how hummingbirds can improve their nutrient gain through learned selective feeding, where individuals can learn to stay in the area or move on depending on the quality of tested flowers. Researchers tested this with two species of hummingbird: the broad-tailed hummingbird (selasphorus platycercus) and the rufous hummingbird (S. rufus), in mountainous parts of Colorado.
interpretation_notes: Squares represent flights when hummingbirds accepted/fed from a flower, and circles represent flights following rejection of a flower. Conclusion: hummingbirds can "improve net energetic returns above random expectations"() by moving away from already/recently depleted flowers and staying closer to non-depleted sources.

title: Unexpected redwood mortality from synergies between wildfire and an emerging infectious disease
citation: Metz, M. R., Varner, J. M., Frangioso, K. M., Meentemeyer, R. K., & Rizzo, D. M. (2013). Unexpected redwood mortality from synergies between wildfire and an emerging infectious disease. Ecology, 94(10), 2152–2159.
methods_summary: Researchers used comparisons of condition of areas of redwood forests infected by the fungal pathogen causing sudden oak death, with areas not affected. They do this to examine novel interactions between infectious plant diseases and fire, most of which seemed to be caused by climate change.
interpretation_notes: Altered disturbance regimes, mostly due to climate change, have led to unexpected interacting negative effects on coastal redwoods. SOD (Sudden Oak Death) is a fungal pathogen affecting various species of oak trees, especially in the coastal areas of California. Coastal redwood forests include various levels, from understory to canopy. Redwood trees stretch up very tall into the canopy layer, while shorter trees such as Tanoaks live in the understory. Researchers have found that oak trees in coast redwood forests can be infected by SOD and die, they leave behind dead, dry wood. Due to climate change, fires have become more common and extreme. Oaks killed by SOD are burning more often, and that fire can spread up the dead trees into the younger parts of the redwood canopy (that are more vulnerable to fire), effectively killing redwoods at a higher rate.

title: Energetic Benefits of Communal Roosting by Acorn Woodpeckers during the Nonbreeding Season
citation: du Plessis, M. A., Weathers, W. W., & Koenig, W. D. (1994). Energetic Benefits of Communal Roosting by Acorn Woodpeckers during the Nonbreeding Season. The Condor, 96(3), 631–637.
methods_summary: Researchers examined the benefits and consequences of communal roosting in Acorn Woodpeckers (Melanerpes formicirvorus) during the non-breeding season when populations rely most on decreased nutrient/cached (collected and stored for later) acorns. They found that roosts inside of preferred trees in the Quercas genus, or Oak trees, were around 4.3 C warmer than the outside enrvionmental temp, and each individual that joined a communal roost then raised the roost temperature by an additional 1.2 C.

title: Energetic efficiency of foraging mediates bee niche partitioning.
citation: Balfour, N. J., Shackleton, K., Arscott, N. A., Roll-Baldwin, K., Bracuti, A., Toselli, G., & Ratnieks, F. L. W. (2021). Energetic efficiency of foraging mediates bee niche partitioning. Ecology, 102(4), 1–7.
methods_summary: Researchers interested in the coexistence of bumble bees () and honey bees () examined the SMR's (speed:mass ratio) of several species of each. They found that SMR accounted for around 74% of the variation in visits to 22 different flower species between bumble bees and honey bees. The differences could be explained by the fact that, " Bumble bees visited flowers at a greater rate (realizing greater energy benefits) than honey bees, but were heavier (incurring greater energy costs) and predominated only on plant species where their benefit : cost ratio was higher than for honey bees,"(). Furthermore, as neither bumble bee nor honey bee outcompeted each other, researchers could conclude that niche partitioning is important to their continued coexistence.

title: Biodiversity Consequences of Predation and Host Plant Hybridization on an Aphid-Ant Mutualism
citation: Wimp, G. M., & Whitham, T. G. (2001). Biodiversity Consequences of Predation and Host Plant Hybridization on an Aphid-Ant Mutualism. Ecology, 82(2), 440–452.
taxa: Insects; Hemiptera; Aphids; Hymenoptera; Ants; Plants
methods_summary: Researchers were interested in studying the mechanisms behind the relationship between the aphid species, Chaitophorus populico, which is only found within a certain proximity (with a decline of around 88% at >6m) of ants. Host plant species and quality for the aphids also had an effect on aphid numbers, but ant presence was the largest deciding factor. The scientists tested aphid densities on trees, as well as potted plants, at different distances from the ant mounds. The mechanism between the two species seems to be of mutual benefit: where ants protect the aphids from predators with their presence, and in turn the ants receive nutritional benefits through "tending" the aphids to get access to their secreted honeydew.

title: Morphological variability in tree root architecture indirectly affects coexistence among competitors in the understory
citation: Aschehoug, E. T., & Callaway, R. M. (2014). Morphological variability in tree root architecture indirectly affects coexistence among competitors in the understory. Ecology, 95(7), 1731–1736.
methods_summary: To examine the differences in interactions within the plant community, especially between understory plants, scientists experimentally altered different morphological traits of Quercus douglasii, or Blue Oaks. Depending on whether the Blue Oaks were altered to have more or less shallow root systems factored into whether they facilitated the presence of invasive annual grasses, a big problem in California. It also affected how well they did against neighbors/competitiors, e.g. overall leaf and seed production, and biomass.

title: Analysis of an evolutionary species-area relationship
citation: Losos, J. B., & Schluter, D. (2000). Analysis of an evolutionary species-area relationship. Nature, 408(6814), 847–850. https://doi.org/10.1038/35048558
methods_summary: The authors analyzed the species–area relationship using an evolutionary framework that incorporates processes such as speciation and extinction. Species richness was plotted against area using a scatter plot to examine how evolutionary processes contribute to differences in biodiversity across areas of different sizes. The figure is meant to represent long-term patterns rather than short-term ecological measurements.
interpretation_notes: The points in the scatter plot represent outcomes predicted by an evolutionary model, not measurements from a single field experiment. The figure reflects long-term processes like diversification and extinction rather than immediate ecological interactions.

title: Predator Diet Breadth Influences the Relative Importance of Bottom‐Up and Top‐Down Control of Prey Biomass and Diversity
citation: Jiang, L., Morin, P. J., Editor: Jonathan B. Losos, & Associate Editor: Michel Loreau. (2005). Predator Diet Breadth Influences the Relative Importance of Bottom‐Up and Top‐Down Control of Prey Biomass and Diversity. The American Naturalist, 165(3), 350–363. https://doi.org/10.1086/428300
methods_summary: Jiang and Morin conducted a controlled experiment using simple aquatic prey communities. They compared three treatments: no predator (control), a specialist predator (Euplotes), and a generalist predator (Stentor). They measured prey biomass and prey diversity under each treatment to test how predator diet breadth influences top-down control.
interpretation_notes: “Control” means no predator was added to the system. “Euplotes” is a specialist predator that feeds on a limited range of prey species, while “Stentor” is a generalist predator that feeds on many prey species. The height of each bar represents the average prey biomass or prey diversity remaining after the experiment.

title: The ecology of infectious disease: effects of host diversity and community composition on Lyme disease risk
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
citation: K. LoGiudice, R.S. Ostfeld, K.A. Schmidt, & F. Keesing, The ecology of infectious disease: Effects of host diversity and community composition on Lyme disease risk, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 100 (2) 567-571, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0233733100 (2003).
topic: Communities: Predation; Communities: Parasitism and Disease
methods_summary: The authors developed a model of Lyme disease transmission that includes different vertebrate host species with different abilities to infect ticks. The model examines how the density of white-footed mice and the presence of other host species affect the proportion of infected tick nymphs.
interpretation_notes: The x-axis shows white-footed mouse density (number of mice per hectare), and mice are important hosts that infect many ticks. Each panel (A–F) represents different combinations of host species in the community, and the colored lines show hosts with different abilities to transmit the pathogen to ticks. In the bar graph, dilution potential represents how much each host species can reduce Lyme disease infection in ticks, where taller bars indicate species that contribute more to lowering disease risk.

title: Linking long-term dietary patterns with gut microbial enterotypes
citation: Wu, G. D., Chen, J., Hoffmann, C., Bittinger, K., Chen, Y. Y., Keilbaugh, S. A., Bewtra, M., Knights, D., Walters, W. A., Knight, R., Sinha, R., Gilroy, E., Gupta, K., Baldassano, R., Nessel, L., Li, H., Bushman, F. D., & Lewis, J. D. (2011). Linking long-term dietary patterns with gut microbial enterotypes. Science (New York, N.Y.), 334(6052), 105–108. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1208344
methods_summary: Researchers collected gut microbiome samples and dietary information from human subjects. They compared microbial community composition between individuals consuming low-fat diets and high-fat diets using microbial DNA sequencing and statistical analysis of community similarity.
interpretation_notes: In panel A, each point represents one person’s gut microbiome community. Points that cluster together have more similar microbial compositions. PC1, PC2, and PC3 are statistical axes summarizing differences among microbial communities. In panel B, weighted distance measures how different microbial communities are from each other. Higher values indicate greater differences in microbial community composition. Blue bars compare Day 1 samples to later samples, while red bars compare samples collected between later days. Subjects are grouped into low-fat diet and high-fat diet categories.

title: Wolves Modulate Soil Nutrient Heterogeneity and Foliar Nitrogen by Configuring the Distribution of Ungulate Carcasses
citation: Bump, J.K., Peterson, R.O. and Vucetich, J.A. (2009), Wolves modulate soil nutrient heterogeneity and foliar nitrogen by configuring the distribution of ungulate carcasses. Ecology, 90: 3159-3167. https://doi.org/10.1890/09-0292.1
topic: Food Webs and Production; Nutrient Cycling
methods_summary: The sites of 17 moose carcasses, killed in winters between 2002-2004 and verified to have come from wolf predation, were sampled a series of times (late May-early June 2004, spring 2005, and spring 2006) to analyze soil nutrient contents of phosphorus, nitrogen, and potassium in Isle Royale National Park, Michigan. At each site, two soil cores were taken from the center of the carcass, defined using the rumen and hair mat left behind from the animal, and two additional soil cores were extracted at approximately 6 meters away from the center on each side. Due to site marking limitations, site number decreased over time as the exact locations of sites were unable to be redetermined in subsequent years.
interpretation_notes: Inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium are all macronutrients in soil that reflect on its general fertility and capacity for support for plant life. Asterisks show significant differences at the P < 0.05 level.

title: Sea Otters and Kelp Forests in Alaska
citation: Estes, J.A. and Duggins, D.O. (1995), Sea Otters and Kelp Forests in Alaska: Generality and Variation in a Community Ecological Paradigm. Ecological Monographs, 65: 75-100. https://doi.org/10.2307/2937159
topic: Communities, Disturbance, and Succession; Food Webs and Production
taxa: Mammals; Mustelids; Algae; Brown algae; Kelp
methods_summary: Several sample sites in the Aleutian Islands and southeast Alaska (4 with abundant otters, 2 without otters, 1 in a transitional state) were each sampled one time each--some in the summer of 1987 and some in the summer of 1988 in order to determine the effects of a trophic cascade involving algae, sea urchins, and sea otters in different environments. Sites were randomly chosen and urchins from within quadrats at sites were collected and measured until 200 individuals were collected or 20 quadrats were assessed.
interpretation_notes: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which eat algae and kelp. dV/dt represents the rate of change in biomass-dependent plant production for the solid line. Students must be able to figure out that the dashed lines represent the rate of consumption of algal biomass by sea urchins, categorized by otter abundance.

title: Population Density and Species Composition of Moss-Living Tardigrades in a Boreo-Nemoral Forest
citation: Jönsson, K.I. (2003), Population density and species composition of moss-living tardigrades in a boreo-nemoral forest. Ecography, 26: 356-364. https://doi.org/10.1034/j.1600-0587.2003.03458.x
topic: Communities, Disturbance, and Succession; Communities: Diversity
methods_summary: Mosses from a boreo-nemoral forest site in southeastern Sweden was sampled in July of 2000 to determine tardigrade diversity in mosses growing under different conditions. From a section of spruce forest, 74 samples were taken and 18 different species of mosses were found. From a section of clear-cut forest, 27 samples were taken and 10 different species of mosses were found. Parts of these samples were used to extract tardigrades, after which the animals were collected via micropipette, identified, and counted. The sections of the moss samples were then dried for a week and weighed to determine their dry weight.
interpretation_notes: There are multiple different species of tardigrade, and different species of tardigrade can coexist and live on one species of moss. Tardigrade abundance is measured as tardigrade count per gram of dry moss.

title: Vegetation Development on a Dated Series of Abandoned Lead and Zinc Mines in Southwestern Wisconsin
citation: Kimmerer, R W (1984). Vegetation development on a dated series of abandoned lead and zinc mines in southwestern Wisconsin. Am. Midl. Nat.; (United States), 111:2. https://doi.org/10.2307/2425328
methods_summary: This study explores the effects of succession in abandoned mining sites to determine the relationships between waste pollution and successional plant growth. Ten abandoned mine sites in the Upper Mississippi Zinc and Lead district were selected intentionally due to their known dates of abandonment minimal disturbace to experienced after being abandoned. About 180 random quadrats per site were observed for species and estimated total cover, then verified with point frame estimates.
interpretation_notes: A forb is "any herbaceous plant that is not a grass" (according to dictionary.com). Annual, biennial, and perennial refer to the plant's lifespan and regrowth cycles wherein annual plants complete their lifecycle over the span of one year, biennials complete their life cycle over the course of two years, and perennials persist over multiple years.

title: The Ecology of the Merriam Kangaroo Rat (Dipodomys Merriami Mearns) on the Grazing Lands of Southern Arizona
citation: Reynolds, H.G. (1958), The Ecology of the Merriam Kangaroo Rat (Dipodomys merriami Mearns) on the Grazing Lands of Southern Arizona. Ecological Monographs, 28: 111-127. https://doi.org/10.2307/1942205
methods_summary: This study was conducted to achieve a comprehensive study on the Merriam kangaroo rats and their ecological role. Kangaroo rats were captured using snap traps over the span of November 1942 to September 1943 and March-November 1946 in the Santa Rita Experimental Range in Arizona. Snap traps, each active for 3 consecutive nights, were laid in straight line transects, laid on randomized mechanical intervals relative to roads.
interpretation_notes: The figure represents a cross section of the geography of the study area, which is around 30 miles south of Tuscon, Arizona.

title: The Role of Disturbance in the Pattern of a Riparian Bryophyte Community
citation: Kimmerer, R. W., & Allen, T. F. H. (1982). The Role of Disturbance in the Pattern of a Riparian Bryophyte Community. The American Midland Naturalist, 107(2), 370–383. https://doi.org/10.2307/2425387
methods_summary: A vertical sandstone cliff in southwestern Wisconsin on the upper Kickapoo River was studied using 27 quadrats, which were randomly placed within the range of typical flooding (the lower 1.5m of the cliff face). The quadrats were studied in the summer and autumn of 1977 and the spring of 1978. Total cover was determined according to subunit and percent cover was caluculated across whole quadrats, in order to study bryophyte responses to natural disturbances.
interpretation_notes: C. conicum, F. obtusifolius, G. aeruginosum, and B. rutabulum are all different species of moss, subject to disturbance via floods.
